o: Its rostrum is continuous below with the lamina terminalis

The thin rostrum curves down and back from the genu to join the lamina terminalis.
So the corpus callosum and lamina terminalis together close the front of the third ventricle region. (Last's p. 586)
Fibres of the genu curve forward as the forceps minor

Genu fibres sweep forward into the frontal lobes, forming the forceps minor.
They form the roof of the anterior horn as they pass. (Last's p. 586)
Fibres of the splenium curve backward as the forceps major

Splenium fibres curve back symmetrically to the occipital lobes as the forceps major.
The forceps major raises the bulb of the posterior horn. (Last's p. 586)
Its fibres form the tapetum in the wall of the posterior and inferior horns

As callosal fibres turn into the temporal and occipital lobes they form the tapetum.
The tapetum forms the roof and lateral wall of the posterior horn and the lateral wall of the inferior horn. (Last's p. 586)
Lies in the posterior wall of the third ventricle

It lies in the anterior wall, embedded in the upper part of the lamina terminalis.
The posterior commissure is the one in the posterior wall, below the pineal.
Connects olfactory regions and the anterior parts of the temporal lobes

It links the olfactory areas and the anterior (middle and inferior) temporal gyri of the two sides.
It is a commissure of the old and the newer cortex.
Is the main commissure joining the two hippocampi

The hippocampi are joined by the hippocampal commissure between the crura of the fornix.
That lies under the splenium, well behind the anterior commissure.
Has the columns of the fornix passing down just behind it

The columns of the fornix curve down behind the anterior commissure, in front of the interventricular foramina.
They then pass through the hypothalamus to the mamillary bodies.
Begins as the fimbria of the hippocampus

Hippocampal efferent axons gather as the alveus, then the fimbria, which becomes the crus of the fornix.
The crus arches up behind the thalamus under the splenium.
Has a body lying under the corpus callosum, attached to the septum pellucidum

The two crura join under the corpus callosum to form the body.
The septum pellucidum stretches between the body of the fornix and the corpus callosum.
Ends mainly in the mamillary bodies

Most fibres of the columns end in the mamillary body, a key link in the Papez circuit.
From there the mamillothalamic tract runs to the anterior thalamic nucleus.
Consists of commissural rather than association fibres

Last's stresses the opposite: the fornix is an association tract rather than a true commissure.
Only the small hippocampal commissure crosses between the crura.

questions.s: Concerning the hippocampus and inferior horn:
o: The hippocampus forms the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle

The hippocampus bulges into the floor (and medial wall) of the inferior horn.
It is a rolled-in part of the parahippocampal gyrus.
The pes hippocampi lies at the posterior end of the inferior horn

The expanded, ridged pes hippocampi is at the anterior end of the hippocampus, near the tip of the horn.
Posteriorly the hippocampus narrows into the fimbria and crus of the fornix.
The amygdaloid body lies in the floor of the inferior horn behind the hippocampus

The amygdaloid body lies in the roof at the tip of the inferior horn, just above the pes hippocampi.
It sits at the end of the tail of the caudate nucleus. (Last's p. 591-2)
The hippocampus is supplied mainly by the anterior cerebral artery

It is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery, with help from the anterior choroidal artery.
The anterior cerebral supplies the medial surface above the corpus callosum.
Is separated from the lentiform nucleus by the external capsule

The internal capsule separates caudate and thalamus from the lentiform nucleus.
The external capsule lies between the putamen and the claustrum.
Has a tail that lies in the floor of the inferior horn

The tail runs in the roof of the inferior horn, getting thinner as it goes forward.
The floor of the inferior horn is the hippocampus. (Last's p. 591-2)
Forms the corpus striatum together with the globus pallidus alone

Caudate and putamen together form the (neo)striatum; the globus pallidus is the pallidum.
The corpus striatum as a whole is caudate plus lentiform nucleus.
Has the amygdaloid body at the extremity of its tail

At the end of the tail, in the roof of the inferior horn, is the amygdaloid body.
It makes a slight bulge just above the pes hippocampi. (Last's p. 591-2)
Has its globus pallidus lateral to the putamen

The globus pallidus is the medial, paler part; the putamen is lateral.
The putamen is continuous with the head of the caudate below the anterior limb of the internal capsule.
Is supplied largely by lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery

The lateral striate (lenticulostriate) arteries pass up through the anterior perforated substance.
They are the arteries of cerebral haemorrhage, and also supply the internal capsule.
Lies medial to the internal capsule

It lies lateral to the internal capsule.
The caudate and thalamus lie medial to the capsule.
Is related laterally to the external capsule and claustrum

Lateral to the putamen are the external capsule, the claustrum, the extreme capsule and the insula.
The insula lies deepest in the lateral sulcus.
Has its anterior limb between the head of caudate and the lentiform nucleus

The anterior limb separates the caudate head from the lentiform nucleus.
It carries frontopontine fibres and thalamic fibres to and from the frontal lobe.
Has its posterior limb between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus

The posterior limb separates thalamus (medially) from lentiform nucleus (laterally).
It carries corticospinal and thalamocortical sensory fibres.
Carries corticonuclear fibres through the genu

Corticonuclear fibres to the motor cranial nerve nuclei run in the genu.
Corticospinal fibres for arm, hand, trunk and leg follow behind in the posterior limb. (Last's p. 585)
Has corticopontine fibres as its smallest fibre group

Corticopontine fibres, about 20 million, are the largest group in the internal capsule.
Clinically, the corticospinal and sensory fibres matter more. (Last's p. 585)
The optic radiation passes through the anterior limb

The optic radiation passes through the retrolentiform part, behind the lentiform nucleus.
It then sweeps back in the lateral wall of the posterior horn.
The auditory radiation passes through the retrolentiform part

The auditory radiation runs in the sublentiform part, below the lentiform nucleus.
It goes from the medial geniculate body to the transverse temporal gyri.
In the posterior limb, fibres for the leg lie in front of those for the arm

The order from front to back is arm, hand, trunk, leg, then perineum.
The head fibres are further forward, in the genu. (Last's p. 585)
Thalamocortical fibres to the postcentral gyrus pass in the posterior limb

Sensory radiations from the ventral posterior thalamus run in the posterior limb behind the motor fibres.
So a capsular lesion often gives hemianaesthesia as well as hemiplegia.
Arises from the lateral geniculate body

Fibres of the optic tract synapse in the lateral geniculate body, which gives rise to the optic radiation.
The radiation is also called the geniculocalcarine tract.
Carries fibres for the lower visual field in its loop into the temporal lobe

The temporal (Meyer's) loop carries fibres from the lower retina, which see the upper field.
A temporal lobe lesion therefore gives an upper quadrantanopia.
Lies in the medial wall of the posterior horn

It lies in the lateral wall of the posterior horn, against the tapetum.
The calcar avis is in the medial wall.
Ends in the superior temporal gyrus

It ends in the visual cortex (area 17) around the calcarine sulcus.
The superior temporal gyrus receives the auditory radiation.

questions.s: Concerning lesions of the visual pathway:
o: A lesion of the optic chiasma typically causes a homonymous hemianopia

A central chiasmal lesion cuts the crossing nasal fibres, giving a bitemporal hemianopia.
A pituitary tumour is the classic cause.
A lesion of the right optic tract causes a left homonymous hemianopia

The right tract carries fibres from the right half of each retina, which see the left field.
So the left half of both visual fields is lost.
The macula is represented at the anterior end of the visual cortex

The macula registers at the posterior end of the visual area, near the occipital pole.
Peripheral retina is represented progressively further forward. (Last's p. 587)
Each visual cortex registers the opposite field of vision

Each visual area receives from its own half of each retina, so it registers the opposite field.
Upper and lower fields are also crossed. (Last's p. 587)
Has its anterior pole at the interventricular foramen

All four surfaces converge to the small blunt anterior pole at the interventricular foramen.
The pole is covered in ependyma.
Has its lateral surface related to the internal capsule

The lateral surface is bevelled by the internal capsule.
Thalamocortical fibres stream out from it into the capsule.
Has part of its superior surface in the floor of the lateral ventricle

An oblique strip along the lateral margin of the superior surface lies in the lateral ventricle.
This strip, covered in ependyma, belongs rather to the hemisphere.
Is always joined to its fellow by an interthalamic adhesion

The interthalamic adhesion is present in only about 60% of brains.
When present it crosses the third ventricle and is not a true commissure. (Last's p. 593)
The anterior nucleus receives the mamillothalamic tract and projects to the cingulate gyrus

Mamillary body to anterior thalamic nucleus to cingulate gyrus is part of the limbic (Papez) circuit.
The cingulate gyrus is part of the limbic lobe.
The medial geniculate body is concerned with hearing

It relays auditory fibres from the inferior colliculus to the auditory cortex.
The auditory radiation runs in the sublentiform internal capsule.
The ventral posterior nucleus receives the medial and spinal lemnisci

Ascending sensory lemnisci end in the ventral posterior nuclei.
These relay to SmI in the postcentral gyrus.
The lateral geniculate body relays visual fibres

Most optic tract fibres synapse in the lateral geniculate body.
Some fibres bypass it to the pretectal area and superior colliculus for reflexes.

questions.s: Concerning the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary:
o: The supraoptic nucleus mainly produces oxytocin

The supraoptic nucleus mainly produces vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone).
Oxytocin comes mainly from the paraventricular nucleus. (Last's p. 569)
Neurosecretory material travels along the axons at about 3 cm a day

It travels at about 3 mm a day to the pars nervosa.
There it is stored and released into capillaries. (Last's p. 569)
The pars distalis receives its releasing factors along nerve fibres

Releasing factors reach the pars distalis through the hypophyseal portal vessels.
Only the posterior lobe gets hypothalamic nerve fibres.
The mamillary bodies receive the columns of the fornix

The columns of the fornix end mainly in the mamillary bodies.
The mamillary bodies lie in the floor of the third ventricle, in the interpeduncular fossa.
Has a pars distalis making up about a quarter of the gland

The pars distalis is about 75% of the gland.
The pars nervosa forms most of the rest. (Last's p. 569)
Has a pars nervosa containing about 100 000 unmyelinated fibres

These fibres come from the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei.
They form the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract down the infundibulum. (Last's p. 569)
Has an anterior lobe developing from the floor of the diencephalon

The anterior lobe develops from Rathke's pouch, an upgrowth from the roof of the stomodeum.
The posterior lobe is the downgrowth from the diencephalon.
Has its stalk passing through the diaphragma sellae

The infundibulum pierces the diaphragma sellae, the dural roof of the pituitary fossa.
A pituitary tumour bulging up through it may press on the optic chiasma.
Has the lamina terminalis as its anterior wall

The lamina terminalis runs from the optic chiasma up to the rostrum of the corpus callosum.
The anterior commissure is embedded in it.
Has a roof formed by the fornix alone

The roof is ependyma, with the tela choroidea and choroid plexuses above.
The fornix lies above the tela choroidea, not in the ventricle wall.
Communicates with the fourth ventricle through the interventricular foramen

It joins the fourth ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct.
The interventricular foramina join it to the lateral ventricles.
Has the pineal recess in its anterior wall

The pineal and suprapineal recesses are in the posterior wall.
The optic and infundibular recesses are in front and below.
Has the corpus callosum forming the roof of its anterior horn and body

Callosal fibres pass across the anterior horn and body, forming their roof.
In the posterior and inferior horns the tapetum takes over. (Last's p. 586)
Has the septum pellucidum forming the medial wall of its anterior horn

The septum pellucidum separates the two anterior horns.
It stretches from the corpus callosum to the fornix.
Has the calcar avis in the medial wall of its posterior horn

The calcar avis is a ridge produced by the calcarine sulcus.
If well developed it can obliterate the posterior horn.
Has choroid plexus in its anterior and posterior horns

There is no choroid plexus in the anterior or posterior horns.
The plexus runs along the choroid fissure in the body and inferior horn only.
Has a total volume of about 500 ml

The total volume is about 130 ml.
More than 500 ml is produced each day, so it turns over several times. (Last's p. 614)
Is produced entirely by the choroid plexuses

About 30% comes from brain capillaries, seeping in via the extracellular fluid.
The choroid plexuses produce the rest. (Last's p. 614)
Has about 100 ml in the ventricles

The ventricles hold about 30 ml; the subarachnoid space holds about 100 ml.
Of the subarachnoid CSF, about 75 ml is spinal and 25 ml cranial. (Last's p. 614)
Has a normal pressure of about 130 mm of water

Pressure is about 130 mm of water lying on the side.
The 1500 g brain weighs only about 50 g floating in it. (Last's p. 614)
The superior peduncle carries most efferent fibres from the dentate nucleus

Dentatorubral and dentatothalamic fibres leave through the superior peduncle.
They cross in the midbrain to the opposite red nucleus and thalamus.
The middle peduncle consists of pontocerebellar fibres

Pontine nuclei send fibres across the midline into the opposite middle peduncle.
It completes the corticopontocerebellar pathway.
The anterior spinocerebellar tract enters through the superior peduncle

The anterior spinocerebellar tract climbs to the upper pons and turns back in the superior peduncle.
The posterior tract enters through the inferior peduncle.
The superior peduncles decussate in the pons

They decussate in the midbrain, at the level of the inferior colliculus.
The decussation is seen centrally in sections at that level.
The flocculonodular lobe is the neocerebellum

It is the archicerebellum, mainly vestibular in its connections.
The neocerebellum is the large lateral part of the hemispheres.
Lesions cause ataxia and intention tremor but not paralysis

Cerebellar lesions disturb movement and balance: ataxia, intention tremor, nystagmus, dysarthria.
There is no paralysis. (Last's p. 617-18)
A unilateral lesion causes signs on the opposite side of the body

A cerebellar hemisphere affects the same side of the body.
Its pathways cross twice, so signs are ipsilateral.
The neocerebellum evolved with the cerebral hemispheres

The neocerebellum developed with the growing complexity of the hemispheres (cerebral mechanisms).
The palaeocerebellum serves spinal mechanisms.

questions.s: At the level of the superior colliculus the midbrain shows:
o: The red nucleus in the tegmentum

The red nucleus is the naked-eye feature of the tegmentum at superior colliculus level.
Fibres of the oculomotor nerve sweep through it.
The trochlear nucleus

The trochlear nucleus lies at inferior colliculus level.
The oculomotor nucleus is at superior colliculus level.
The decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles

This decussation is seen at inferior colliculus level.
It lies centrally in the tegmentum.
The substantia nigra dorsal to the aqueduct

The substantia nigra lies ventrally, between tegmentum and crus.
The tectum is the only part dorsal to the aqueduct.
The abducent nucleus lies in the upper pons

It lies in the lower pons, under the facial colliculus.
The trigeminal motor nucleus is in the mid pons.
Pontine nuclei send fibres into the middle peduncle of the same side

Pontocerebellar fibres cross the midline before entering the opposite middle peduncle.
This gives the transverse fibres of the basilar pons.
The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve lies in the medulla

The trigeminal motor nucleus is in the mid pons.
The spinal trigeminal nucleus extends down into the medulla and upper cord.
The facial colliculus overlies the abducent nucleus

Facial nerve fibres loop over the abducent nucleus, raising the facial colliculus.
So a lesion here can give both VI and VII palsy.
Each pyramid contains about a million fibres

Each pyramid holds about a million fibres, of which about 700 000 are small myelinated fibres.
These are corticospinal fibres. (Last's p. 612)
About 85% of pyramidal fibres cross in the motor decussation

They form the lateral corticospinal tract.
The uncrossed rest descend mainly as the anterior corticospinal tract. (Last's p. 612)
The inferior olivary nucleus projects to the opposite cerebellum

Olivocerebellar fibres cross and enter the opposite inferior cerebellar peduncle.
The olive is the bulge lateral to the pyramid.
The hypoglossal nerve emerges between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle

XII emerges between the pyramid and the olive.
IX, X and XI emerge behind the olive.
Posterior column fibres cross in the spinal cord

They ascend on the same side and synapse in the gracile and cuneate nuclei.
The internal arcuate fibres cross in the medulla to form the medial lemniscus.
Most anterolateral tract fibres synapse in the reticular formation

Only about 10% go directly to the thalamus; 90% synapse in the reticular formation.
This is the spinoreticulothalamic pathway. (Last's p. 624)
The fasciculus gracilis carries fibres from the upper limb

Gracilis carries the lower limb and lower trunk; cuneatus carries the upper limb.
Cuneatus is present only above about T6.
Vibration sense travels in the posterior columns

Vibration is tested with a 128 Hz tuning fork and travels with position sense.
So it is lost with posterior column disease. (Last's p. 623)
Has about 40% of its fibres from the motor area

About 40% come from MsI; the rest from widespread cortex, including sensory areas.
So it is not purely a motor area output. (Last's p. 612)
Has no more than 2% of its fibres from Betz cells

The giant pyramidal cells of layer V give no more than 2%.
These few are the fibres that synapse directly on motor neurons. (Last's p. 603)
Ends mostly on interneurons rather than directly on motor neurons

About 98% synapse on interneurons in laminae VII and VIII.
These then project to lamina IX motor neurons. (Last's p. 625)
Has over half its fibres ending in the cervical cord

About 55% end at cervical and T1 levels for the upper limb.
20% go to the trunk and 25% to the lower limb. (Last's p. 625)
Preganglionic sympathetic cells lie in the lateral horn from T1 to L2

The lateral horn holds sympathetic cells from T1 to L2.
Parasympathetic cells sit at S2–4. (Last's p. 621-2)
The substantia gelatinosa is lamina IX

The substantia gelatinosa is lamina II.
Lamina IX contains the motor neurons.
White rami communicantes arise from every spinal nerve

White rami come only from T1 to L2, where there are lateral horn cells.
Every spinal nerve gets a grey ramus.
The adult cord ends at L3

The adult cord ends at about L1 (L1/2).
It ends at L3 at birth and reaches the adult level by about 20 years. (Last's p. 575)

questions.s: Blood supply of the spinal cord:
o: The anterior spinal artery arises from the basilar artery

It forms from a branch of each vertebral artery.
The two branches unite in front of the medulla.
The arteria radicularis magna arises most often at T10 or T11 on the left

It can arise anywhere from T7 to L4, but slightly more often at T10/11 and on the left.
It is the main supply to the lower anterior cord. (Last's p. 626)
The posterior spinal arteries supply the anterior two-thirds of the cord

The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds.
The posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior columns and horns.
Radicular arteries reinforce the spinal arteries along the cord

Without radicular feeders the longitudinal arteries could not supply the whole cord.
Their number varies, which makes some segments watershed zones.

questions.s: Concerning spinal cord and meningeal levels:
o: At birth the cord ends at about L3

At birth it ends at L3 and reaches the adult L1 level by about 20 years.
In the fetus it reaches S2. (Last's p. 575)
The dural sac ends at S2

Dura, arachnoid and subarachnoid space all end at S2.
The filum terminale pierces the sac there. (Last's p. 574-5)
The cervical enlargement corresponds to segments C5–T1

These segments lie opposite vertebrae C3–T1.
They supply the upper limb plexus. (Last's p. 619-20)
The lumbosacral enlargement lies opposite vertebrae L2–S3

Segments L2–S3 lie opposite vertebrae T9–L1.
Segments are higher than their vertebrae because the cord is shorter than the column. (Last's p. 619-20)
The recurrent artery of Heubner is a branch of the middle cerebral artery

It comes from the anterior cerebral artery near the anterior communicating artery.
It is absent in about 3%. (Last's p. 601)
The anterior choroidal artery is a branch of the posterior cerebral artery

It is a branch of the internal carotid artery.
The posterior choroidal arteries come from the posterior cerebral.
The visual cortex is supplied wholly by the middle cerebral artery

The visual area lies within the posterior cerebral territory.
Middle cerebral branches may reach far enough back to supply the macular area. (Last's p. 600)
Most subarachnoid haemorrhages come from circle of Willis aneurysms

About 90% of subarachnoid haemorrhages are due to such aneurysms.
Common sites are the anterior communicating and posterior communicating junctions. (Last's p. 599-600)
The great cerebral vein drains into the straight sinus

The great cerebral vein (of Galen) joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus.
It is formed by the two internal cerebral veins.
The superficial middle cerebral vein drains into the superior sagittal sinus

It runs along the lateral sulcus and drains into the cavernous sinus.
Anastomotic veins link it to the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses.
The basal vein begins on the convexity of the hemisphere

The basal vein begins at the anterior perforated substance.
It winds round the cerebral peduncle to join the great cerebral vein.
Cerebral veins have valves

Cerebral veins and dural sinuses are valveless.
So infection can spread along them in either direction.
The leg area of the motor cortex is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery

The paracentral lobule, with leg and perineum areas, lies in anterior cerebral territory.
So ACA occlusion gives a contralateral leg weakness. (Last's p. 600)
Broca's area is supplied by the middle cerebral artery

The speech areas lie in middle cerebral territory on the lateral surface.
Left MCA occlusion often causes aphasia.
The visual area is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery

Area 17 lies within the posterior cerebral territory.
PCA occlusion gives a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.
The auditory area is supplied by the middle cerebral artery

The transverse temporal gyri lie within the lateral sulcus, in MCA territory.
The cochleae are bilaterally represented, so one lesion does not cause deafness.
